title: Hardware for the Job
learningIntention: I can explain how hardware specifications affect performance and select appropriate hardware for a particular task.
teacherIntroduction: Hardware is the physical equipment in a digital system. Its specifications — such as processing, memory, storage and display — affect how well it can do a job. Today we will compare teacher-prepared hardware cards against two tasks, explain how a specification would affect performance, and select appropriate hardware for each task. We will not use student accounts or collect personal data.
childActivity: Compare teacher-prepared hardware cards, explain how one specification would affect performance, and select appropriate hardware for two given tasks.
reflectionPrompt: Which specification made the biggest difference to your choice, and why?
movementMoment: Stand in two task zones while you hold up or point to the hardware card you would select for that task, then return to your seat to write a short reason.
stoppingPoint: We stop after selecting hardware for two tasks and explaining one specification. We do not collect names or personal data.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can name a specification, say how it would affect performance, and justify a hardware choice for a given task. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A first Years 7–8 Digital Technologies lesson that extends earlier work on system components, using cards or a teacher screen only.

title: Data as Numbers
learningIntention: I can investigate how digital systems represent text, image and audio data using integers.
teacherIntroduction: Digital systems store and work with data as integers — whole numbers. Today we will investigate how a short piece of text, a simple image and a simple sound can each be represented with integers, using a teacher-provided table and grids. We will not use student accounts, photos of students, or personal recordings.
childActivity: Represent a short piece of text, a simple image and a simple sound as integers, then say what stayed the same and what was lost.
reflectionPrompt: What was gained by representing text, image and audio as integers, and what was lost?
movementMoment: Three corners: move to Text, Image or Audio when the teacher names that kind of data, then point to the integers that represent it.
stoppingPoint: We stop after representing all three kinds of data as integers and discussing one gain and one loss. No student photos, names or recordings are collected.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can show integers for text, image and audio, and name one thing that stayed the same or was lost. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A Years 7–8 unplugged data-representation lesson, useful after students can already say that the same data can be shown in more than one way.

title: Why Binary?
learningIntention: I can explain how and why digital systems represent integers in binary.
teacherIntroduction: Binary uses only two digits, 0 and 1. Digital systems use it because hardware can represent two clear states, such as off and on. Today we will convert a few integers to binary and back, then explain how and why a digital system would use binary. We will not need student devices or accounts.
childActivity: Convert a few integers to binary and back, then explain how and why a digital system represents integers in binary.
reflectionPrompt: Why might a digital system use two states, rather than ten, to represent integers?
movementMoment: Show 0 or 1 with arms down or up when the teacher points to each place value in a binary number, then sit and write the integer.
stoppingPoint: We stop after converting a few integers and explaining how and why binary is used. No student data is collected.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can convert at least one integer to binary and give a reason why two states are useful. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A Years 7–8 unplugged lesson after Data as Numbers, or a short standalone lesson on binary.

title: Trace the Algorithm
learningIntention: I can trace an algorithm to predict output for a given input and to identify errors.
teacherIntroduction: To trace an algorithm is to follow it step by step, keep track of the values, and predict the output before we trust the result. Today we will trace a short teacher-prepared algorithm, predict the output for a given input, and find an error. We will work on paper or the board. No student accounts or personal data are needed.
childActivity: Trace a short algorithm, predict the output for a given input, then identify and correct an error.
reflectionPrompt: Which step revealed the error, and how did the trace help you find it?
movementMoment: One student, or the teacher, walks the steps of the algorithm on the board while the class calls the current value at each step.
stoppingPoint: We stop after a predicted output has been checked and one error has been identified and corrected. No student data is collected.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can record a trace, state a predicted output, and point to an error. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A Years 7–8 unplugged algorithms lesson that extends earlier work on following steps and decisions.

title: Design an Algorithm
learningIntention: I can design an algorithm involving nested control structures and represent it using a flowchart and pseudocode.
teacherIntroduction: A nested control structure is a decision or a repeat placed inside another decision or repeat. Today we will design a short algorithm for a school task, include one nested structure, and represent the same algorithm as a flowchart and as pseudocode. We will stay on paper or the board, with no student accounts.
childActivity: Design a short algorithm with one nested decision or repeat, then show it as a flowchart and as pseudocode.
reflectionPrompt: What is the nested structure in your algorithm, and why did you put it there?
movementMoment: Trace your flowchart with a finger or a pen while a partner reads the pseudocode aloud, then swap.
stoppingPoint: We stop after one algorithm has been shown both as a flowchart and as pseudocode, with a nested structure labelled. No student data is collected.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can point to a nested structure and show the same algorithm in both representations. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A Years 7–8 unplugged design lesson after Trace the Algorithm, using paper, a board or a teacher screen.

title: What Data Is Essential?
learningIntention: I can investigate the digital footprint an existing system collects and assess if the data is essential to its purpose.
teacherIntroduction: A digital footprint is the data a system collects and keeps about people who use it. Today we will investigate a teacher-prepared description of an existing kind of system, sort the data it collects into essential and not essential for its purpose, and suggest one way the footprint could be managed. We will not log into anything, and we will not investigate a student's own footprint, name, or account.
childActivity: Investigate a teacher-prepared system description, sort the data it collects into essential and not essential, and suggest one way to manage the footprint.
reflectionPrompt: Which collected item was not essential to the purpose, and how could that footprint be managed?
movementMoment: Point, or move a card, to Essential or Not essential as each data item is read, then sit to write one management step.
stoppingPoint: We stop after sorting the prepared data items and suggesting one way to manage the footprint. We do not collect student names, accounts or personal data, and we do not inspect anyone's real footprint.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can classify at least one item as essential or not, and suggest one management step, using only the prepared example. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A Years 7–8 privacy lesson using only a fictional or generic system description prepared by the teacher.

title: Evaluate a System for a User
learningIntention: I can define and decompose a real-world problem with design criteria and a user story, and evaluate an existing system against them.
teacherIntroduction: A user story describes a user by role, what they need, and why. Design criteria are the tests we will use to judge a solution. Today we will define a simple school problem, decompose it into parts, write one user story and two or three design criteria, then evaluate an existing system — on paper or on the teacher's screen only — against those tests, including a possible future impact. We will not use student names, logins or personal data.
childActivity: Write a user story and design criteria for a school problem, then evaluate an existing system against them and note one possible future impact.
reflectionPrompt: Did the existing system meet the criteria and the user story? What future impact should be considered?
movementMoment: Thumbs up, sideways or down for each design criterion as it is checked, then stand if you can name one possible future impact.
stoppingPoint: We stop after the existing system has been evaluated against the user story and criteria, including one possible future impact. No student names, logins or personal data are collected.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can state a user story, at least two design criteria, a judgement against them, and one possible future impact. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A later Years 7–8 lesson that brings problem definition and evaluation together, using a paper mock or the teacher's shared screen only.
